articles.title: Brewers ride ridiculous, record-setting eight-run inning to dominant 3-0 World Series lead over Rays
articles.summary: Jackson Chourio's four-hit night and Robert Gasser's historic shutout outing powered the Milwaukee Brewers to a commanding 3-0 World Series lead.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers moved one step closer to their first ever World Series title on Monday night, taking a 3-0 series lead with a dominant 10-1 win. That's the short version of the story. The long version? The Tampa Bay Rays will be kicking themselves over a disastrous top of the fifth inning, and historians will one day use a clip of that inning, and the entire 2026 Brewers' postseason run for that matter, as proof of how powerful luck is in Major League Baseball. Game three meant the series shifted to Tampa Bay, and Tropicana Field was packed to the rafters with Rays fans and a sizable contingent of Brewers supporters. But as has typically been the case this postseason, only those in Milwaukee blue and gold had much to cheer about. MILWAUKEE BREWERS' DOMINANT BULLPEN AND CLUTCH OFFENSE PUT THE TAMPA BAY RAYS ON THE BRINK At least defensively, the Rays put up a fight. In the top of the second, outfielder Chandler Simpson made a tremendous running catch in the left field corner, crashing into the fence to rob Sal Frelick of a hit. Then catcher Nick Fortes caught Garrett Mitchell trying to steal second base to end the inning. It was all downhill from there. In the third inning, the Milwaukee superteam machine kicked into high gear. Jackson Chourio started things off with a ground ball single. Jake Bauers followed with a walk. That's when the Brewers' incredible penchant for outperforming on batting average on balls in play reared its gigantic head yet again. Christian Yelich popped up a 71 mph blooper that fell in for an RBI single. William Contreras followed with another 79 mph blooper that fell in to drive in the second run of the game. Still, a 2-0 game in the third inning wouldn't normally mean that much, but the Brewers had Robert Gasser on the mound. Who's Robert Gasser you might be wondering? Well, essentially the epitome of a league average pitcher, someone who had a 4.27 "expected" ERA in the regular season, then turned into a Cy Young candidate in the playoffs. Because baseball. Gasser entered his game three start with just one run allowed in the playoffs, but the Rays couldn't muster even that on Monday night. Rarely getting swings and misses, Gasser relied on his best friend in October: the opposing team having exceptionally poor luck on batted balls put in play. Prior to Monday, opposing hitters had just a .185 BABIP against him. Then he went six shutout innings with just three strikeouts and only one hit allowed. How? Because the Rays had an .071 BABIP. Gasser will likely end his postseason with just seven hits on 55 balls put in play, an incredible .127 batting average allowed, when league average is around .300. Gasser's start was the first time a lefty had gone six shutout innings while facing the minimum number of hitters in the World Series since Sandy Koufax. Next time you want your favorite team to acquire the big name starting pitcher in free agency or at the trade deadline, just remember that one of the most effective starters on the team that won the World Series was Robert Gasser. That he did something that hadn't been done in the World Series by a lefty since one of the greatest pitchers in the history of the sport. In large part because of BABIP. There's no luck in baseball, because everything must have an explanation, no matter how absurd. Gasser didn't need much support, obviously, but the Brewers unstoppable offense provided it anyway. In the fifth inning, Milwaukee put together one of the most absurd innings you'll ever see, and a near-perfect reminder of the immense amount of variance and randomness inherent in baseball. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE It started innocently enough, with Chourio once again singling with one out. Jake Bauers flew out for the second out, then Christian Yelich walked to put runners at first and second. Then, the play that will haunt Rays fans forever. William Contreras grounded one in the hole between second and third, and third baseman Junior Caminero went to second base for the force out, unable to see that he had plenty of time to get Contreras at first. But Yelich beat the throw out, loading the bases for Brice Turang. Then, the floodgates opened. Turang hit a grounder to short that Taylor Walls couldn't make the play on, scoring two. Then Garrett Mitchell slapped another single through the infield, directly where the shortstop typically plays. 5-0 Milwaukee. Cooper Pratt followed with a grounder that somehow clipped the foul line for a double, making it 7-0. Sal Frelick hit a soft line drive that fell in to left field to make it 8-0. David Hamilton, having an incredible postseason after a career of being a very bad hitter, drove in the ninth run of the game with a single. Finally, Jackson Chourio added his fourth hit of the game and second of the inning to make it 10-0. Why not? THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! That fifth inning was the first eight-run inning in World Series history. The Brewers went 9-18 with runners in scoring position, had a .471 BABIP and 16 hits against a typically strong Rays pitching staff. Tampa's BABIP? .130. That's only half of it. Per the league's Statcast page, Milwaukee's expected batting average in the game was .254. Their actual batting average was .390. Tampa's expected batting average was .236, and their actual was .107. And that's been Milwaukee's luck all postseason. The Rays added a meaningless garbage time run in the bottom of the ninth, but Milwaukee takes a commanding 3-0 series lead, and is well on their way to the organization's first ever championship. Potentially as soon as Tuesday night's game four. Should the Brewers close it out with a fully rested bullpen, they'd become the first team in the history of the sport to sweep both the NLCS and World Series. They're 10-1 in the playoffs thus far, with a chance to go 11-1 and win ten of nine straight to win a title. Baseball-ruining superteam indeed. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Not all of these results are down to luck, of course, and it's hardly a criticism of the Brewers' team or players to say they've had fortune on their side in the playoffs. Every team that wins the playoff tournament in Major League Baseball has luck go their way. The Dodgers in 2024 and 2025 had plenty of breaks, as did the Rangers in 2023 and Astros in 2022. And the Braves in 2021 and so on. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD But there's an inescapable conclusion from this World Series, and the whole postseason, as a matter of fact: there is no way to "ruin" baseball. Or build a superteam. Or guarantee a championship. Because at the end of the day, the gaps between teams are so small that a few bounces either way over a short series can, and often does, determine the outcome. Having a rotation filled with Cy Young level pitchers is great and all, except that when it comes down to it, Robert Gasser can become Sandy Koufax over 15 innings. There's no way to predict who will get hot, who will be cold, and which teams will have luck on their side. Which is what baseball has always been, and always will be. No matter how much fake complaining owners do.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Jackson Chourio, still just 22, continues his incredible postseason run with 4-hit game in Brewers' Game 3 victory
articles.summary: In Milwaukee's 10-1 rout, Chourio became the youngest player in 80 years to record four hits in a World Series game.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Go ahead, throw whatever pitch you want. Jackson Chourio is ready to hit it.

The ludicrously talented Brewers leadoff man was front and center on Monday at Tropicana Field as Milwaukee made all kinds of history en route to a 10-1 rout of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series . Chourio's contribution to the Fall Classic record books: Still five months away from his 23rd birthday, he became the youngest player in 80 years to record four hits in a World Series game. Two of them came in a neverending fifth inning in which the Brewers scored eight runs, all with two outs — also a World Series record.

The sudden blowout achieved in a single frame set the stage for a truly remarkable scene: Brandon Woodruff — the longest-tenured Brewer, unfathomably just three months removed from the second shoulder surgery of his career — taking the mound in the ninth inning to a raucous ovation from the contingent of Milwaukee supporters who made up a sizable portion of the sellout crowd of 40,388. Woodruff delivered the memorable finale to yet another comprehensive Brewers postseason victory.

For the third game in a row, the 22-year-old led off with a single, hammering a 97.5-mph fastball from former teammate Freddy Peralta into center field. Peralta eventually escaped the first frame unscathed, but he was not so fortunate a couple of innings later. In their second showdown, the right-hander tried something different, but Chourio was unbothered, scalding a first-pitch curveball into left field for a one-out single and coming around to score Milwaukee's first run of the game on a Christian Yelich bloop base hit. William Contreras then drove in another run to make it 2-0 Brewers.

That 2-0 lead felt fairly sturdy given how Brewers starter Robert Gasser was throwing. After Yandy Díaz led off the game with a scorching single, Gasser breezed through an antsy Rays lineup with minimal trouble. He needed 25 total pitches to cruise through the second, third and fourth innings without allowing a baserunner. By the end of his night, Gasser had delivered one of the best outings by a rookie in World Series history — six scoreless innings with one hit allowed — even if it was largely outshadowed by the unprecedented offensive outburst in the fifth inning.

And who started that historic rally? Take a wild guess.

In the fifth, Chourio arrived at the plate with one out as Peralta prepared to navigate the relentless Brewers batting order for a third time. His heater and breaking ball had already been hit hard by Chourio; perhaps Peralta's terrific offspeed pitch would do the trick?

Nope. After coaxing a whiff on a four-seam fastball and misfiring a sweeper way outside, Peralta tried to land a low changeup. But Chourio struck again, lacing a single up the middle.

"Some of the best hands I've ever seen in the batter's box," designated hitter Andrew Vaughn said of Chourio. "Maybe one of the best right-handed swings I've ever seen. I mean, I compare it to Pujols, Miggy — he's special, and he's so young. He's 22 years old, going out there having at-bats like he does, leading off in the World Series like it's nobody's business."

What could've been a harmless, one-out base hit turned out to be the opening salvo of an offensive inning for the ages. After Jake Bauers flied out to left for the second out, the next seven consecutive Brewers batters reached base, chasing Peralta from the game along the way. It was 9-0 Milwaukee by the time Chourio stepped back into the batter's box for his second at-bat of the inning — this time against reliever Cole Sulser — and he wanted in on the RBI parade.

The veteran right-hander got Chourio to a 2-2 count with cutters and four-seamers before trying a sweeper. Chourio tracked the horizontal movement to the outer half and ripped his barrel to the ball, connecting cleanly for the fourth time of the night on a fourth different pitch. This time, the ball soared into the right-center-field gap for a double — Chourio's first extra-base hit of the World Series. Not since 20-year-old St. Louis Cardinals catcher Joe Garagiola in Game 4 in 1946 had a hitter younger than Chourio collected four hits in a World Series game.

"That's what I've been witnessing my whole career," Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski said. "I've watched him forever, it feels like. I think I realized he was different whenever we were in Double-A. … It wasn't just me. Everyone in our organization was like, 'Holy cow, this dude's different.' He's special."

With at least one more at-bat to come, Chourio had a shot at even more exclusive history. Only two players of any age have recorded a five-hit game in the World Series. One of those was Albert Pujols' legendary three-homer performance in Game 3 in 2011 , which also included a pair of singles. The other was Paul Molitor, who notched five hits in the last World Series Game 3 Milwaukee had played before Monday, back in 1982. But Chourio's bid to join the Hall of Fame duo fell short in the seventh, when first-base umpire Vic Carapazza ruled that he didn't check his swing on a Garrett Cleavinger slider, concluding Chourio's night with a strikeout to go with his four knocks.

"He's just so talented," hitting coach Daniel Vogelbach said. "I think people forget how young he is — he could be playing college baseball right now. He works so hard. But he's just such a good kid. He's the right kid. He doesn't care about getting the accolades. We're playing a sim game before getting ready for the World Series, and he's cheering like a little kid for his teammates, and that's what makes him so special. He just plays so relaxed every day."

The 10-0 score held nearly to the end of the game, until Díaz roped a garbage-time RBI double off Woodruff with two outs in the ninth. Milwaukee happily settled for a 10-1 final score and a 3-0 series lead.

On a roster filled with savvy trade acquisitions, underrated hidden gems and late-blooming breakouts, Chourio occupies a category unto himself. He received a $1.8 million bonus as one of top players in his international amateur class when he signed with the Brewers out of Venezuela as a 16-year-old in 2021, yet it didn't take long for that bonus to look like a bargain.

By the next year, when Chourio was rocketing through the minors as a teenager, it was clear Milwaukee had landed not just a good player but also a potential game-changer. The Brewers' confidence in Chourio's transcendent trajectory was evident in their enormous commitment to him, inking the top prospect to an eight-year, $82 million extension before he had played a major-league game. Since then, he has been terrific, and he's still only scratching the surface

"You hear about him, and it's like, ah, he's just a little 18-year-old. I see him on the backfield in spring training, I'm like, 'Yeah, I'd probably dominate him, whatever,'" Woodruff said of his first impressions of Chourio.

"So I got to face him in the scrimmage game the other day, and I always talk a lot of crap to him. Like, 'You don't know what it was like before the shoulder thing, dude — I would own you" ... knowing in the back of my mind, like, this kid, he's pretty good. … I got him two strikes, and then he singled off of me."

That Chourio reemerged as a main character in Game 3 of the World Series should come as no shock. After all, he was the one who delivered the first big swing of this downright dominant Brewers run to the precipice of the first championship in franchise history.

Twenty-three days ago, the Brewers were down 2-0 in the third inning of NLDS Game 1 against the Padres when Chourio smashed a game-tying, two-run homer off Robbie Ray that sizzled off his bat at 113.3 mph, the hardest-hit home run of his young career. The next night, Chourio won an epic encounter with San Diego super-closer Mason Miller, roping a walk-off single that turned a 3-2 deficit into a 4-3 victory . Chourio was quieter in the NLCS against Los Angeles but still managed to deliver one of the series' signature swings: a first-pitch ambush of Blake Snell to lead off Game 3 at Dodger Stadium with a home run.

For Chourio, the hits kept coming once the Fall Classic began. Any concern about the Brewers dealing with rust after a week off before Game 1 evaporated when Chourio jumped on a first-pitch cutter from Nick Martinez for a leadoff single and came around to score Milwaukee's first run of the World Series. Facing one of the best arms in the American League in Drew Rasmussen in Game 2, Chourio made sure the Brewers responded quickly to the Rays' early 4-0 lead, notching a leadoff knock to spark the latest Milwaukee comeback . In Game 3, no comeback was necessary. It was just a barrage of Brewers batters doing their thing, with Chourio once again leading the charge.

"Nobody's surprised that Jack Jack's doing this," manager Pat Murphy said afterward. "He's understanding what it takes, the discipline that it takes. He's coming into his own. Nobody's shocked."

articles.title: World Series 2026: Christian Yelich turns pivotal play as Brewers' under-the-radar hero of Game 3 — 'The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe'
articles.summary: By beating a throw to second, Yelich flipped a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime for Milwaukee.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.

Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.

It was a shellacking of historic proportions.

But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.

Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The Fox graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.

Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.

The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.

But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.

"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewers manager Pat Murphy insisted afterward. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."

Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled to 4-0.

As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berserk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."

Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.

Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.

"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.

That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.

With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Vilade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.

"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."

It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.

"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.

Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.

"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.

On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.

Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.

"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."

"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."

"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."

Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.

The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

articles.title: B/R's All-MLB Team Roster for the 2026 Season
articles.summary: It's time to highlight the best and brightest across Major League Baseball during the 2026 season with Bleacher Report's All-MLB Team.
articles.body:
It's time to highlight the best and brightest across Major League Baseball during the 2026 season with Bleacher Report's All-MLB Team.

The roster consists of one player at each position, five starting pitchers and two relief pitchers, with the three outfielders chosen from the full pool of outfielders and not specific to any one position. Players were selected based solely on their 2026 production.

Our panel of voters was made up of the following MLB experts:

Nine of the 16 selections were unanimous, and ultimately there was a clear consensus for B/R's 2026 All-MLB roster.

Catcher: Gabriel Moreno, Arizona Diamondbacks

Stats: 143 OPS+, .311/.388/.486, 50 XBH (16 HR), 83 RBI WAR: 6.7

Gabriel Moreno became just the fifth catcher in MLB history to win a batting title with his .311 batting average, joining Bubbles Hargrave (1926), Ernie Lombardi (1938, 1942), Joe Mauer (2006, 2008, 2009) and Buster Posey (2012).

The 26-year-old had 33 doubles, 16 home runs and 83 RBI while hitting primarily out of the No. 3 and No. 4 spots in the Arizona lineup, and he batted .304 with runners in scoring position.

The former Gold Glove winner also threw out 25.0 percent of base-stealers and graded out as one of the better pitch-framers in baseball, providing well-rounded value.

First Base: Pete Alonso, Baltimore Orioles

Stats: 149 OPS+, .267/.363/.522, 67 XBH (43 HR), 113 RBI WAR: 4.9

Not much went right for the Orioles in a season that started with playoff aspirations and ended with a 79-82 record and a potential retooling on the horizon after Adley Rutschman was traded at the deadline.

That said, the five-year, $155 million deal they gave Pete Alonso in free agency went exactly as hoped, with the longtime Mets slugger leading the AL in home runs (43) and RBI (113) while logging a career-high 149 OPS+ and playing in all 161 games.

Yankees slugger Ben Rice deserves a mention here, but he spent more time at designated hitter than he did at first base, while Alonso made 142 starts at the position.

Second Base: Brice Turang, Milwaukee Brewers

Stats: 124 OPS+, .268/.366/.450, 61 XBH (21 HR), 100 RBI, 19 SB

Brice Turang backed up his breakout 2025 campaign with an even better year at the plate this season, setting career-high marks in doubles (37), home runs (21), RBI (100), runs scored (102) and OPS+ (124).

With that middle-of-the-order offensive production alongside his elite defensive metrics ( 23 DRS, 14 OAA ), he was one of the most valuable players in the sport, with his 7.3 WAR trailing only Pete Crow-Armstrong (9.8) and Cristopher Sánchez (8.1).

The Brewers were baseball's best team during the regular season, and Turang was their best everyday player.

Others Receiving Votes: Brandon Lowe, PIT (1 vote)

Third Base: Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays

Stats: 144 OPS+, .276/.360/.524, 68 XBH (42 HR), 101 RBI WAR: 5.7

Still only 23 years old, Junior Caminero has firmly established himself as one of the game's premier power threats with back-to-back 40-homer, 100-RBI seasons in the middle of the Tampa Bay lineup.

He also took a significant step toward becoming a more complete hitter this year, raising his walk rate (6.3 to 11.3 percent) and on-base percentage (.311 to .360) while maintaining a strikeout rate below 20 percent.

There's a good chance he will finish runner-up to Yordan Alvarez in AL MVP balloting, and he has been the driving force for a Rays team that won 98 games and has reached the World Series.

Shortstop: Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals

Stats: 125 OPS+, .281/.359/.441, 52 XBH (18 HR), 54 RBI, 45 SB WAR: 6.7

Despite hitting a career-low 18 home runs, Bobby Witt Jr. was once again one of baseball's best all-around players with an elite combination of offensive impact, defensive skills and game-changing speed.

His 45 steals ranked third in the majors, he scored 94 runs for a Royals team that averaged just 4.3 runs per game and his 10.6 percent walk rate was a career-high while setting the table out of the No. 2 spot in the lineup.

All of that coupled with stellar defensive metrics (8 DRS, 24 OAA) and highlight-reel glove work that also passes the eye test helped him eclipse the 6-WAR mark for the third consecutive season.

Others Receiving Votes: Elly De La Cruz, CIN (1 vote)

Outfield: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Chicago Cubs

Stats: 156 OPS+, .280/.372/.570, 84 XBH (45 HR), 107 RBI, 41 SB WAR: 9.8

Two years removed from posting an 88 OPS+ and looking like a glove-first center fielder in his first full season in the big leagues, Pete Crow-Armstrong was baseball's most valuable player with a staggering 9.8 WAR season.

He tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs and backed that power production with 41 steals, becoming the seventh member of baseball's illustrious 40/40 club while also leading the league in OPS+ (156), runs scored (119) and total bases (357).

That offensive season alone would be enough to make him a unanimous selection for the All-MLB team, but he was also arguably the best defensive player in all of baseball. His elite defensive metrics ( 16 DRS, 25 OAA ) should win him a second straight Gold Glove and could make him the 2026 NL Platinum Glove winner.

Outfield: Randy Arozarena, Seattle Mariners

Stats: 148 OPS+, .281/.381/.484, 62 XBH (26 HR), 79 RBI, 26 SB WAR: 5.7

Another year, another 20/20 season from Randy Arozarena.

The 31-year-old has now rattled off six in a row dating back to his 2021 AL Rookie of the Year campaign, and this year it came alongside a career-high 148 OPS+ thanks in part to a .381 on-base percentage that ranked fifth on the AL leaderboard.

He had an AL-leading 113 runs scored and a career-high 5.7 WAR over 154 games, and earned his third All-Star selection along the way.

All of that makes for a well-timed first trip to free agency this winter, and a nine-figure payday should be waiting as arguably the most impactful bat on the market.

Outfield: Fernando Tatis Jr., San Diego Padres

Stats: 130 OPS+, .289/.358/.470, 60 XBH (25 HR), 83 RBI, 38 SB

After a glacial start to the season offensively, Fernando Tatis Jr. was as productive as any hitter in baseball after the All-Star break.

1st Half: 416 PA, .277/.340/.374, 25 XBH (5 HR), 139 TB

2nd Half: 288 PA, .307/.385/.610, 35 XBH (20 HR), 155 TB

That late surge helped propel the Padres into the playoff picture, and as usual his dynamic power-speed production was accompanied by stellar defense in right field.

He also took on a semi-regular role at second base, starting 50 games at the position to give San Diego some welcome flexibility.

Others Receiving Votes: Andy Pages, LAD (2 votes), James Wood, WAS (1 vote)

Designated Hitter: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros

Stats: 190 OPS+, .316/.432/.601, 77 XBH (42 HR), 106 RBI WAR: 6.8

Yordan Alvarez made a serious run at the Triple Crown, ultimately taking home the AL batting title (.316) while finishing second in home runs (42) and RBI (106). That is widely expected to win him AL MVP honors.

One of the best pure hitters in baseball, he also led the AL in on-base percentage (.432), slugging percentage (.601), OPS+ (190) and walks (109) while piling up 6.8 WAR even with 134 of his 158 games coming at designated hitter.

He hit a ridiculous .355/.558/.731 with runners in scoring position, and he was the only player in baseball with a walk rate above 15 percent and a strikeout rate below 20 percent.

Starting Pitcher: Jacob Misiorowski, Milwaukee Brewers

Stats: 30 GS, 16-5, 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 252 K, 174.2 IP WAR: 6.5

The hardest-throwing starting pitcher in baseball history, Jacob Misiorowski threw 1,677 four-seam fastballs during the regular season and averaged 100.6 mph while generating a 40.2 percent whiff rate with the high-octane pitch.

He showed flashes of ace-caliber upside as a rookie while earning an All-Star selection, but inconsistent command relegated him to the bullpen in October. With Freddy Peralta traded, he became the de facto ace of the staff and responded by slashing his walk rate (11.4 to 6.6 percent) while breaking through as one of baseball's most dominant pitchers.

The NL leader in ERA (1.80), WHIP (0.80) and strikeouts (252) is likely headed for unanimous NL Cy Young honors, and the Brewers have him under club control through the 2031 season.

Starting Pitcher: Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees

Stats: 33 GS, 14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP WAR: 7.0

Cam Schlittler made his MLB debut midway through the 2025 season and became a household name during last year's postseason when he tossed eight shutout innings against the rival Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series.

With Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón sidelined to start the year and Max Fried also missing time during the first half, he broke through as the ace of the staff for the Yankees and put together a dominant season.

He limited opponents to a .163 average and piled up 126 strikeouts with his upper 90s fastball, and he was one of only seven pitchers to record at least 20 quality starts. AL Cy Young honors likely await during award season.

Starting Pitcher: Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves

Stats: 27 GS, 14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP

If not for one ugly start against the Angels in April (4.0 IP, 5 H, 2 BB, 6 ER), Chris Sale might be a more serious threat to Jacob Misiorowski in the NL Cy Young conversation.

The 37-year-old did not allow more than three earned runs in any of his other 26 starts, posting a 1.87 ERA over 158.2 innings in those outings, and he closed out the year with a run of nine straight quality starts before going 5.2 innings in his final outing.

His 6.5 strikeout-to-walk ratio led the majors by a sizable margin over Jacob Misiorowski (5.7) and Drew Rasmussen (5.4), and his 2.16 ERA overall was better than his 2024 NL Cy Young campaign.

Starting Pitcher: Cristopher Sánchez, Philadelphia Phillies

Stats: 33 GS, 18-7, 2.91 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 231 K, 207.0 IP WAR: 8.1

Cristopher Sánchez led all pitchers with 8.1 WAR during the 2026 season, and much of that value stemmed from a dominant stretch early in the year where he rattled off a streak of 50.2 scoreless innings.

The 29-year-old earned the starting nod in the All-Star Game while going 12-3 with a 2.23 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 135 strikeouts in 121 innings. He was not as dominant during the second half, but still put together another terrific overall campaign.

With back-to-back 8-WAR seasons in the books, he has established himself as one of the game's true frontline starters.

Starting Pitcher: Dylan Cease, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 29 GS, 11-6, 2.40 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 239 K, 169.0 IP WAR: 5.5

Despite a lackluster 4.55 ERA and 1.33 WHIP for the Padres in 2025, the Blue Jays shelled out a massive seven-year, $210 million contract to sign Dylan Cease in free agency, and it looks like money well spent.

The 30-year-old reached 200 strikeouts for the sixth consecutive season while slashing his ERA by more than two full runs, and he allowed just 108 hits in 169 innings for a .180 opponents' batting average.

With the AL lead in FIP (2.56), hits per nine innings (5.8) and strikeouts per nine innings (12.7), he should show up on plenty of AL Cy Young ballots and could finish runner-up to Cam Schlittler.

Others Receiving Votes: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, LAD (2 votes), Drew Rasmussen, TB (1 vote), Tarik Skubal, DET/LAD (1 vote)

Relief Pitcher: Mason Miller, San Diego Padres

Stats: 66 G, 38/41 SV, 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 16.6 K/9, 70.0 IP WAR: 3.1

Mason Miller struck out 129 of the 272 batters he faced this season and recorded 28 straight saves to open the year before his first blown save at the beginning of August.

He averaged 101.4 mph with his fastball and generated a ridiculous 56.3 percent whiff rate with his slider, overpowering hitters with two of the single most effective pitches in baseball.

There were some rumblings that he might hit the trade block before the Padres surged back into contention, and his status as a potential trade chip could be a major storyline again this offseason.

Relief Pitcher: Louis Varland, Toronto Blue Jays

Stats: 71 G, 35/37 SV, 1.27 ERA, 1.00 WHIP, 11.2 K/9, 78.0 IP WAR: 3.6

The Blue Jays acquired Louis Varland in a four-player deal with the Twins at the 2025 trade deadline in a move that didn't receive much fanfare at the time, but by October he was the team's most reliable bullpen arm during their run to the World Series.

He began the 2026 season in a setup role, but took over ninth-inning duties at the end of April and turned in a dominant season that earned him an All-Star selection and vaulted him into the upper echelon of closers.

With club control through the 2030 season, that 2025 deadline deal is quickly shaping up to be one of the most lopsided trades in recent memory, especially when you consider what the Padres had to give up to acquire Mason Miller.

Others Receiving Votes: Bryan Baker, TB (1 vote)

articles.title: New MLB Rumors on Shohei Ohtani's Injuries, Dodgers' Handling of Star Amid Struggles
articles.summary: After being swept out of the playoffs in the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, the Los Angeles Dodgers are now facing questions about the missteps that hindered them from completing a World Series title three-peat.
articles.body:
After being swept out of the playoffs in the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, the Los Angeles Dodgers are now facing questions about the missteps that hindered them from completing a World Series title three-peat.

Most notably, the Dodgers' handling of three-time NL MVP Shohei Ohtani fell under the spotlight amid the two-way phenom's injury-riddled campaign.

According to The Athletic's Katie Woo , "Ohtani's determination to pitch and the Dodgers' dubious decision to let him push his return from injury left their best player compromised for the playoffs. Ailments that arose in early summer carried into October, with Ohtani physically absent from the mound and figuratively so from the plate. It was exactly the scenario the Dodgers pledged to avoid, and it ultimately played a key role in their downfall."

Ohtani played in 135 games during the regular season and hit 30 home runs with 81 RBI, his lowest totals since his injury-shortened 2020 campaign with the Los Angeles Angels. He managed to make 14 starts and compiled an 8-2 record with a career-best 1.79 ERA.

Still, Ohtani clearly wasn't himself during the playoffs. He didn't pitch during the postseason, and he hit just .192 with one homer and three RBI across eight games.

Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman acknowledged that the team should have done a better job managing Ohtani's workload to ensure he was at 100 percent for the playoffs.

"How do we manage through a long season and have him at his best going into October? That's a challenge," Friedman said at the Dodgers' end-of-year news conference last week. "We have to figure that out together, and I'm confident that we will continue to learn from things as we go and continue to make it better."

However, when asked what the Dodgers could have done differently or whether Ohtani could pitch a full season and still be effective in October, Friedman admitted, "I don't know the answer to that."

articles.title: MLB's 10 Most Memorable World Series Moments of the Modern Era
articles.summary: From broken curses to walk-off blasts and plenty in between, the modern era of Major League Baseball's World Series history has delivered no shortage of unforgettable moments.
articles.body:
From broken curses to walk-off blasts and plenty in between, the modern era of Major League Baseball's World Series history has delivered no shortage of unforgettable moments.

Not every Fall Classic has been an instant classic, but most of them have given us at least something worth remembering.

However, the most memorable moments naturally occurred in the latter stages of the best-of-seven series that actually went the distance.

For the purposes of this exercise, we're defining the "modern era" as any World Series played a year beginning with a 2. With apologies to the 1985-1993 window that featured a plethora of iconic moments, that's basically ancient history at this point.

After a handful of honorable mentions, we've ranked the 10 most memorable World Series moments of the past quarter century.

In putting together a top 10 from more than 25 years' worth of World Series, there were a lot of things worth jotting down. But these are the seven that were the most difficult to leave out of the top 10, presented in chronological order:

Roger Clemens vs. Mike Piazza, Game 2, 2000 World Series

There was no love lost in the Subway Series, especially between this pair of many-time All-Stars. Clemens drilled Piazza in the head with a pitch earlier in the season, and then he hurled the barrel of Piazza's broken bat back at him in their first meeting of the World Series. Nothing like a little benches-clearing conversation in the Fall Classic.

The Rally Monkey's Biggest Rally, Game 6, 2002 World Series

Down 3-2 in the series and down 5-0 in the seventh inning, things sure looked bleak for the Halos. But they harnessed the power of the rally monkey like never before with a three-run home run by Scott Spiezio in the seventh, a Darin Erstad homer to lead off the eighth and a colossal two-run double by Troy Glaus to take the lead. The Angels went on to win the series in seven.

Álex González's Walk-Off Homer, Game 4, 2003 World Series

The 2003 Marlins had six different position players who ended up receiving votes for NL MVP, but González was not one of them. And prior to hitting this walk-off blast in the 12th inning of Game 4—the only home run he ever hit in 24 career games in the playoffs—he was 5-for-53 in that postseason. Needless to say, nobody saw it coming, and the Yankees were unable to recover from it, proceeding to lose Games 5, 6 and the World Series.

Red Sox End the Curse of the Bambino, Game 4, 2004 World Series

It was an historic moment 86 years in the making, but it was also maybe the most anticlimactic World Series ever? Not only did the Red Sox sweep the Cardinals, but they never trailed for a moment.

Cardinals Walk Off Red Sox on Obstruction Call, Game 3, 2013 World Series

Because the Red Sox bounced back to win each of the next three games and the series, this completely chaotic ending has been kind of forgotten in the sands of time. What initially looked like a 4-2-7-2 inning-ending double play turned into a walk-off win for St. Louis because Will Middlebrooks got his legs tangled up with Allen Craig at third base.

Jorge Soler Launches One Over the Train Tracks, Game 6, 2021 World Series

Officially, this home run traveled 446 feet, which is nothing compared to some of the tape-measure blasts we see annually in the Home Run Derby. But that sure feels like a miscalculation, as Soler cleared the train tracks in left field at what used to be Minute Maid Park. What slim hopes the Astros had of winning this series left the stadium along with that ball.

18th Inning Walk-Off Blasts for the Dodgers in Both 2018 and 2025

What are the odds, right? There have been just two World Series games that lasted more than 14 innings. Both of them were home games for the Dodgers, and both of them ended on walk-off home runs in the 18th inning. Max Muncy delivered the first one against the Boston Red Sox in Game 3 of the 2018 World Series, while it was Freddie Freeman providing the round-tripper in Game 3 of the 2025 World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays.

10. Alex Bregman's Game 5 Walk-Off Single (2017)

Knowing what we now know about the Houston Astros cheating scandal, this one hits a whole lot differently than it did at the time.

In the moment, though, the 2017 World Series between the Astros and the Los Angeles Dodgers was one heck of a fun roller coaster ride, with Game 5 in particular featuring all sorts of corkscrews and loop-de-loops.

In that one, each team had three innings with at least three runs scored, including the Dodgers putting up a three-spot in the top of the ninth to tie the game at 12-12.

All told, there were seven home runs and 16 extra-base hits in a game that took well north of five hours. (All hail the pitch clock.)

But in the bottom of the tenth inning, it was a two-out single by Alex Bregman off Kenley Jansen that broke the tie, both in the game and in the series. The Dodgers bounced back to win Game 6, but Houston prevailed in Game 7.

Bregman was only in his second year in the majors, while Jansen was on the tail-end of a two-year run as the undisputed most dominant reliever in the sport. It was the unofficial moment in which the former truly emerged as a star while the latter was never quite the same again.

9. Scott Podsednik's Walk-Off Home Run (2005)

In the past three decades of MLB history, there have been just 12 instances of a player making enough plate appearances during the regular season to qualify for a batting crown while failing to hit a single home run.

One of those players was Scott Podsednik, who was named an All-Star for the only time in his career while playing in 129 homer-less games in 2005.

What a long con it was, though, setting the stage for perhaps the unlikeliest walk-off home run in postseason history.

It was Game 2 between the Chicago White Sox and Houston Astros, the latter knotting things up with two runs in the top of the ninth inning off Bobby Jenks. José Vizcaíno singled to left and Podsednik was unable to cut down the tying run at the plate.

He made up for that throw with a tater off Brad Lidge, though, as the White Sox won the second of four consecutive games in that World Series sweep.

And poor Lidge, am I right? He had a 2.18 ERA in his postseason career, allowing just two home runs in 45.1 innings pitched. But the two that he allowed came in back-to-back games, this one by Scotty Pods coming one appearance after he let Albert Pujols hit one approximately 1,000 feet in Game 5 of the NLCS.

8. Houston Astros Combined No-Hitter (2022)

There have been more than 700 games played in World Series history.

Only two of them have ended with a zero in the hits column: Don Larsen's perfect game in 1956 and Houston's four-headed gem against the Phillies in Game 4 of the 2022 Fall Classic.

Cristian Javier pitched the first six innings of near perfection with nine strikeouts, putting quite the capstone on what was (by a wide margin) the best season of his career thus far. He did issue one free pass in the second inning and another in the third, but no harm done.

Bryan Abreu, Rafael Montero and Ryan Pressly followed suit with one hitless inning apiece, the latter's eight-pitch walk of Kyle Schwarber the only minor blemish of the bunch.

In the entire game, only one ball hit by the Phillies had an expected batting average north of .320—and even that Jean Segura lineout to Kyle Tucker in the eighth inning was a pretty routine catch by the right fielder. They just never even threatened to put a hit on the board.

Heading into that game in the City of Brotherly Love, the Phillies were leading the series 2-1 with high hopes of celebrating a championship at home after Game 5. However, that no-no turned the series on its ear, Philadelphia managing just three total runs scored while losing the final three games.

7. Freddie Freeman's Walk-Off Grand Slam (2024)

Pardon the semi-spoiler, but what's left on this list is five Game 7s and an iconic Game 6 performance.

Kind of hard for something that happened in Game 1 of a World Series to hold a candle to those do-or-die scenarios.

But the only walk-off grand slam in World Series history certainly made us think about it.

This wasn't just any walk-off grand slam, either.

And the Yankees had just intentionally walked Mookie Betts in order to get a left-on-left matchup of Nestor Cortes vs. Freddie Freeman.

An injured Freddie Freeman, no less, for a Kirk Gibson-esque moment. Freeman hurt his ankle late in the regular season and missed both Games 4 and 6 of the NLCS, entering the World Series with a .461 OPS in eight postseason games played.

A single almost certainly would have been sufficient to win the game, but an out would have resulted in a victory for the Yankees and quite possibly a very different outcome to that World Series.

Freeman jumped all over the first pitch, though, clobbering Cortes' 92 MPH fastball for a no-doubter into the Los Angeles night sky.

It proved to be just the spark he needed, also homering in Game 2, Game 3 and Game 4 en route to becoming one of the easiest picks in the history of World Series MVPs.

6. Howie Kendrick off the Fair Pole (2019)

The theme of the 2019 World Series between the Washington Nationals and Houston Astros was: One for the Road.

That's because for the first time in the combined history of MLB, the NBA and the NHL, the road team won every single game of this backwards best-of-seven series.

For the first six innings of Game 7, home starter Zack Greinke was untouchable. He allowed one single in the second inning, and immediately erased it with a double play ball. That was the full extent of the damage against him until Anthony Rendon hammered a solo shot with one out in the seventh inning to make it a 2-1 ballgame.

When A.J. Hinch went to Will Harris out of the bullpen one batter later, the Cardiac Nats knew their time to shine had arrived.

Fittingly, Howie Kendrick's subsequent lead-flipping two-run home run—AKA hands down the most important moment of the series—would not have been a home run at Nationals Park, per Statcast .

At Minute Maid Park, though, he got just enough to clang one off the fair/foul pole.

What's hard to believe about this one is it arguably wasn't even Kendrick's most iconic moment of the 2019 postseason, considering he also had a 10th inning grand slam in the winner-take-all Game 5 of the NLDS against the Dodgers.

Without that home run, he never gets a chance to hit this one.

But between those two moments and winning NLCS MVP in the middle of them, he'll never need to pay for a drink in the nation's capital.

5. Madison Bumgarner Slays the Royals (2014)

In Game 4 of the 2010 World Series, a 21-year-old southpaw by the name of Madison Bumgarner went eight shutout innings in a San Francisco Giants victory over the Texas Rangers.

Two years later, he put up seven scoreless frames in his lone appearance of the 2012 sweep of the Detroit Tigers.

But it was during the last act of the Even-Year Giants that MadBum etched his name in MLB lore.

In Game 1 of the 2014 World Series, a solo home run in the seventh inning of a 7-0 game was the only damage the Kansas City Royals could muster against him.

In Game 5, he tossed a 117-pitch complete-game shutout.

Three days later, Bumgarner delivered maybe the greatest relief appearance in MLB history.

He entered Game 7 at the beginning of the bottom of the fifth inning, staked to a 3-2 lead. And after allowing an Omar Infante leadoff single, he proceeded to retire the next 14 batters before things got a bit dicey with two outs in the bottom of ninth when center fielder Grégor Blanco misplayed an Alex Gordon single into a "triple."

A mere mortal might have cracked in that moment, especially with Salvador Perez coming to the plate. At any rate, it was Perez who delivered the aforementioned home run in Game 1 of this series—the only run Bumgarner ever allowed in 36 innings pitched in the World Series.

Sorry for the spoiler there, but Bumgarner won the battle, getting Perez to foul out to clinch the World Series. Neither team scored in the final five innings, and he threw 68 pitches to seal the deal.

Every other moment in our top six came from a Game 7.

But David Freese ensuring there would be a Game 7 in the 2011 World Series between the St. Louis Cardinals and Texas Rangers was nothing short of legendary.

The funny thing about Game 6 being remembered as "The David Freese Game" is that through the first 53 outs, it was anything but.

Freese dropped a routine pop-up to start the fifth inning, which led immediately to a run for the Rangers. He also had a combined total of five runners on base through his first four plate appearances, going 0-for-3 with a walk—after thriving to the tune of a .393/.443/.732 line through his first 16 postseason games.

When it mattered the most, though, he brought the lumber.

With two on and two down in the bottom of the ninth inning of a 7-5 game, Freese lifted a 98 MPH Neftalí Feliz fastball over the head of Nelson Cruz in right field and off the wall for a game-tying triple to extend the game.

And after a chaotic 10th inning that produced two runs apiece, Freese led off the bottom of the 11th with a walk-off home run off Mark Lowe.

Just for good measure, he also delivered a two-run double in his first plate appearance of Game 7, polishing off a three-AB sequence for the ages.

3. Luis Gonzalez Series-Winner off Mariano Rivera (2001)

For an entire generation of baseball fans, watching the New York Yankees lose in the postseason has become a darn-near annual rite of passage. They've made the playoffs 21 times in the past 26 years, but with just one World Series trophy (in 2009) to show for it.

Heading into the 2001 World Series between the Yankees and the Arizona Diamondbacks, though, the Bronx Bombers were an October juggernaut.

To fans of the other 29 teams, Derek Jeter, Bernie Williams, Andy Pettitte and Mariano Rivera were the four horsemen of the baseball apocalypse, spearheading an unstoppable Yankees force that had won three consecutive World Series and four of the past five Fall Classics.

So, when Rivera entered in the eighth inning with a 2-1 lead in Game 7, things felt almost hopeless for the underdog—even more so after the Sandman mowed down the Snakes with three swinging strikeouts in his first inning of work.

But when Mark Grace opened the bottom of the ninth with a base hit to center, followed by Rivera committing a throwing error on Damian Miller's sacrifice bunt, it felt like the MLB equivalent of the Rocky IV "He's cut! The Russian is cut!" moment.

Tony Womack tied the game with an RBI double, setting the stage for Luis Gonzalez to deliver the most unforgettable duck snort in the history of the sport.

Call it recency bias if you must, but Game 7 of the 2025 World Series had everything .

The Dodgers and Blue Jays combined to use nine starting pitchers in a winner-take-all extravaganza that featured:

A mammoth home run by a top free agent-to-be (Bo Bichette)

Incredible defense (diving catches by Daulton Varsho and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and a game-saving play by Miguel Rojas immediately before the game-saving play by Andy Pages)

A benches-clearing incident (when Andrés Giménez was drilled by Justin Wrobleski)

Home runs in the eighth (Max Muncy), ninth (Rojas) and 11th innings (Will Smith)

And a World Series-winning double play turned by Mookie Betts as the would-be tying run crossed the plate

If you had to boil the game down to one iconic moment, though, it was the Pages catch, yeah?

We've seen extra innings in Game 7s before.

We've also seen series-extending or series-ending home runs from the unlikeliest of sources.

But with the bases loaded, two outs, tie game, bottom of the ninth inning in Game 7 of the World Series...an outfield collision?!?

In which the player making the historic catch had just been inserted as a defensive replacement five pitches prior ?

Even the script writers in Hollywood would never dream of pitching an idea that absurd, but Pages made it happen.

"I was going to pull a Willie Mays," Kiké Hernández said . "And then [Pages] tackled me, and I felt like I got dunked on, and I thought we lost. I was just down because I thought we lost. And he came up to me and said, 'Are you OK?' 'F--- that, do you have the ball?' He's like, 'Yeah.' I'm like, 'Yeah, let's go!'"

It was the ultimate anti-walk-off moment.

Say this much for Game 7 of the 2016 World Series between the Chicago Cubs and the Cleveland Redacteds: It featured the most unforgettable rain delay in baseball history.

That 17-minute stoppage between the ninth and tenth innings gave everyone a chance to catch their breath. But it also gave Jason Heyward a chance to deliver the exact "rallying the troops" weight room speech that the Cubs needed after blowing what had been a three-run lead in the eighth inning.

Before the skies opened, though, this one was already an instant classic.

Dexter Fowler led off the game with a home run. Javier Báez atoned for two early errors with a solo shot of his own. David Ross homered in what proved to be the final at-bat of his MLB career. And Rajai Davis delivered the ultimate stunner with his game-tying, two-run blast off Aroldis Chapman.

Throw in the rarely-seen two-run wild pitch, the questionable decision to pull Kyle Hendricks in the fifth inning, the even more questionable decision to have Báez bunt with two strikes in the ninth inning and the lengthy championship droughts for each franchise and that rain delay may have just been the world sweating profusely.

In the tenth, Ben Zobrist delivered the tie-breaking double, Miguel Montero provided a much-needed insurance run and the Cubs finally won a World Series 108 years in the making.

articles.title: Jorge Posada Reveals He Doesn't Feel 'Welcome' Around Yankees After Legendary MLB Career
articles.summary: Former New York Yankees star catcher Jorge Posada revealed that he doesn't feel like the organization wants him around anymore.
articles.body:
Former New York Yankees star catcher Jorge Posada revealed that he doesn't feel like the organization wants him around anymore.

"I don't feel welcome when I go there, you know? Even in spring training, I don't feel like — I'm just like, I don't know, like, I don't feel welcome," Posada said during a Tuesday appearance on The Show podcast (h/t Matt Ehalt of the New York Post ). "I don't feel like they want me there, so I don't go."

"I don't know what happened. I'd rather just move forward," he added. "My last season of my career was a really tough one when it comes to handling everything in my part and also the Yankees toward Jorge Posada. So, it's tough to go back and feel that again."

Posada spent his entire playing career on the Yankees from 1995 through 2011, helping them capture four World Series titles.

He earned five All-Star nods and six Silver Slugger Awards throughout his career in New York.

Posada sits at No. 9 on the Yankees' all-time home runs leaderboard while also holding the No. 14 spot on their all-time hits list.

It's worth noting that his final season in New York didn't go smoothly, as he primarily operated as a designated hitter instead of a catcher for the first time in his career.

Still, the Yankees retired Posada's No. 20 in a ceremony in Aug. 2015.

He was also in attendance for New York's spring training ahead of the 2025 season before appearing at the club's Old Timers' Day this year.

It's unknown what caused Posada to feel unwelcome around the Yankees, although he previously explained that the team's mentality needed to change in Aug. 2025.

"It's just more of an attitude than anything," Posada told SNY's Chelsea Sherrod at the time. "They just gotta get a little angry, hopefully a fight or something that happens, not a fight but something that happens to get them going again."

"They need to have that chip on their shoulder," he added. "You've gotta play like that. You can't be friends with everybody."

The Yankees are coming off a 2026 campaign in which they finished with a 93-68 record, but were swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.

articles.title: Miguel Rojas reveals why his Dodgers years meant so much more than baseball
articles.summary: Miguel Rojas thanks the Dodgers for changing his life.As the 2026 MLB season is nearing the end, so is Miguel Rojas’ time on the baseball diamond. Rojas appe...
articles.body:
As the 2026 MLB season is nearing the end, so is Miguel Rojas' time on the baseball diamond.

Rojas appeared as a guest during the Fox pregame show for Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday night and said his time with the Dodgers over the last four years "changed my life."

"They gave me the opportunity to go back home in LA where I made debut 12 years ago …where I had where I had the opportunity to live the best four years of my life in baseball," Rojas said.

Rojas said on the broadcast that he will always cherish the moments the Dodgers organization did for his son son Aaron, like when his teammates would take him to the outfield to shag fly balls.

"He was living the dream for me, and for my daughter, just to be around them. That's what I told the guys," Rojas said. "Thank you for changing my life. And for being part of the best four years of my life."

Rojas' professional baseball career originally began in 2006 when he signed as an amateur free agent from Venezuela with the Cincinnati Reds. In 2012, he became a free agent and signed a minor league deal with the Dodgers.

His MLB Debut came in June 2014. He went on to play in 85 games with the Dodgers.

The next season, he was traded to the Marlins and would spend the next eight years with them.

His second stint with the Dodgers came in 2022 — one of the most important periods in the franchise's history.

Rojas became a World Series hero in 2025 when he hit a solo home run in the ninth inning in Game 7 that propelled the team to winning their second consecutive World Series.

Rojas contemplated retirement after his heroics but decided to stick around for the 2026 season to help the Dodgers attempt a three-peat.

After they were eliminated in the NLCS by the Brewers, he announced his retirement .

Rojas' career finished concluded with two World Series titles, 1,048 hits, .260 batting average and 386 RBIs.

As he is concluding his playing career, he will have one more last ride in baseball.

This winter, Rojas will represent Venezuela in the Professional Baseball League for the Tiburones de La Guaira club.

articles.title: Phillies Named Best Fit for $20 Million Free-Agent Reliever
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Phillies had the worst bullpen ERA of any team in the playoffs during 2026.Outside of closer Jhoan Duran, the Phillies had no consistent hel...
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Phillies had the worst bullpen ERA of any team in the playoffs during 2026.

Outside of closer Jhoan Duran, the Phillies had no consistent help after their reliable starting pitchers. That could soon change this offseason if president of baseball operations, Dave Dombrowski, so desires.

The Athletic's Jim Bowden put together a list of the top 40 free agents in this upcoming class. A name that may have slipped through the cracks is that of the No. 39 player on this list, Jonathan Loáisiga.

Bowden named Philadelphia as one of the best fits for the longtime Yankees reliever.

Why Would the Philadelphia Phillies Want Loáisiga?

The New York Yankees signed Loáisiga from Nicaragua as an international free agent. He made his debut in 2018 with New York and played eight seasons for them. Across those eight seasons (193 games), Loáisiga recorded a 3.54 ERA, although injuries altered his trajectory.

In 2026, Loáisiga signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks , acting as one of their high-leverage relievers. In 67 games, Loásiga recorded a 2.42 ERA. Now, entering his age-32 season, he will re-enter free agency looking to capitalize on his worth.

According to Bowden, the contract prediction for Loáisiga is a two-year, $20 million deal, which the Phillies can obviously afford.

While Loáisiga's ERA was amazing, his advanced stats were even better. According to Baseball Savant, Loáisiga was in the 85th percentile or better in the following stats: pitching run value, fastball run value, xERA, fastball velocity, average exit velocity, chase rate, walk rate, barrel rate, hard-hit rate and ground ball rate.

He didn't strike out many batters, but he made up for it by inducing weak contact and keeping the ball on the ground. While his breaking pitches were average to below-average, teams should be confident in Loáisiga's ability to get hitters out at an elite level, especially the Philadelphia Phillies.

As aforementioned, the Phillies desperately need back-end help other than Duran. While Duran had a 1.82 ERA in 61 games with 33 saves, no other pitcher was reliable enough to count on.

With José Alvarado, Tim Mayza, Brooks Raley, Nestor Cortes, Lou Trivino, José Urquidy and others reaching free agency or arbitration, there's going to be a lot of turnover in the Phillies bullpen.

Alex McFarlane, Jonathan Bowlan, Chase Shugart, Tanner Banks and Duran will likely be the sole survivors of a complete purge.

With Brad Keller likely out the entire 2027 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, the Phillies need an impact arm.

While it may be a little more than fans would expect for Loáisiga, $20 million is a small price to pay to get the team's bullpen into shape.

Dombrowski has a lot of work cut out for him this offseason. From fixing the infield situation to maintaining the bullpen, it will be a busy offseason for Philadelphia.

articles.title: Rays Beat Brewers in Extras to Stay Alive, Box Score Stats, Highlights from 2026 MLB World Series G4
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays will live to see another game in the World Series.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays will live to see another game in the World Series.

With their backs against the wall, the Rays beat the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 in Game 4 of the Fall Classic in a 12-inning thriller on Wednesday, capped off by a walk-off RBI single from Ben Williamson.

Tampa Bay got on the board first, scoring a run in the bottom of the second when Chandler Simpson doubled to right field to drive in Jonny DeLuca.

The Brewers evened things up in the fourth thanks to an RBI double from Cooper Pratt, but the Rays quickly took back the lead in the bottom of the fourth when Junior Caminero scored on an error.

Tampa Bay's lead vanished almost instantly, as David Hamilton hit a solo homer to tie things up in the top of the fifth inning.

After a few scoreless innings for both teams, the Brewers showed some signs of life in the top of the ninth when Pratt got on base with just one out. Garrett Mitchell then hit a ball deep to left field, but a fantastic play from Simpson prevented any damage.

Pratt attempted to steal second and get into scoring position, but he was ruled out after a close play, ending the inning with things still tied up. Aaron Ashby came onto the mound for the Brewers in the bottom of the ninth and retired the side in order, sending things into extra innings.

Neither team could find a run in the 10th or 11th innings, but Pratt delivered the biggest swing of his life in the top of the 12th when he gave the Brewers the lead with a solo home run.

But the Rays didn't go away after the home run.

Caminero reached first base on an error, and Liam Hicks singled up the middle to put runners on the corner with no outs. DeLuca then singled to drive in the tying run and move the winning run into scoring position.

A single from Simpson loaded the bases, and Ben Williamson delivered the walk-off in the form of an RBI single to right field.

The Rays can celebrate for a moment, but they still have an elimination game to play on Wednesday night. Perhaps the momentum from the win in Game 4 will carry into Game 5.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Ben Williamson walks off Brewers in Rays' 12-inning comeback win to avoid sweep in Game 4
articles.summary: After 12 innings, the Rays are still alive.
articles.body: The Tampa Bay Rays still face long odds in the 2026 World Series, but they will fight another day thanks to Ben Williamson. And they just overcame long enough odds on Tuesday.Williamson, the Rays' utility infielder, hit a pinch-hit, walk-off single in the 12th inning of Game 4, allowing the Rays to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Milwaukee Brewers with a 4-3 victory. There will be a Game 5 at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday at Tropicana Field, with Milwaukee leading the series 3-1.BEN WILLIAMSONWALK-OFFRAYS SURVIVE! pic.twitter.com/bjHolx3L4m— MLB (@MLB) October 28, 2026 It was the first walk-off win while facing World Series elimination since David Freese's extra-innings homer in Game 6 of the 2011 Fall Classic, per MLB.com's Sarah Langs.Only a few minutes before the walk-off, Brewers rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt hit what appeared to be the biggest home run in Brewers history, a solo blast in the top of the 12th that put the Brewers up 3-2.COOPER PRATT PUTS THE BREWERS ON THE DOORSTEP! pic.twitter.com/jZejkshf9G— MLB (@MLB) October 28, 2026 The Brewers turned to left-hander Shane Drohan to get the three remaining outs. Drohan failed to record one, partially due to a mistake by the usually strong Milwaukee defense.Leading off the bottom of the 12th, Junior Caminero reached base on a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz, followed by a Liam Hicks single and a Jonny DeLuca RBI single to tie the game. One more single from Chandler Simpson loaded the bases. Then came Williamson, and it was over.No MLB team has ever come back from down 3-0 in the World Series, and it has been done only one time in any seven-game series (the Boston Red Sox in the 2004 ALCS). The Rays would need three more wins to change that.Had the Brewers won Tuesday, it would've been the first World Series sweep since 2012 (San Francisco Giants over Detroit Tigers), and they would've become the first team in MLB history to sweep both the championship series and the World Series. The Rays' win snapped an eight-game postseason winning streak for Milwaukee, which tied an MLB record.The Rays won a marathon gameEven before three rounds of extra innings, Game 4 had enough drama to make it the most competitive game of this series. The Rays struck first in the second inning on a Chandler Simpson double that scored Jonny DeLuca from first base. The Brewers tied the game in the fourth inning on a similar sequence involving Sal Frelick and Pratt, with the rookie notching an RBI double to score Frelick from first. The two teams exchanged another run over the next inning, with Junior Caminero scoring thanks to a missed tag and an errant throw by Brewers third baseman David Hamilton. It's arguable, however, that Caminero benefited from a few more feet of width in the basepath than the rulebook allows. But the Brewers could challenge only whether the tag was made, and they lost. David Hamilton wasn't able to make the tag on Junior Caminero and he ends up scoring after the throwing error to give the Rays the lead in the 4th pic.twitter.com/oJ44uIfWVb— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 28, 2026 In the top of the fifth, Hamilton found immediate redemption with a solo homer off Rays starter Griffin Jax to tie the game. It was only the third home run of this entire World Series.DAVID HAMILTON!WE'RE TIED AGAIN! pic.twitter.com/KyWsGoFz2z— MLB (@MLB) October 28, 2026 At that point, the Rays were facing a dire situation, even in a tie game. With three more games to win, they wanted a long start from Jax. They got only four-plus innings, as he got the hook after Hamilton's homer. The Rays were facing the venerable Milwaukee bullpen, whose top arms all rested in Game 3, thanks to the Brewers' offensive onslaught.The Brewers were also making better contact overall and wound up posting 12 of the 13 hardest-hit balls in the game by exit velocity, per Baseball Savant. It was only by the grace of luck and the Tampa Bay defense that only three of those balls were base hits. But for the remainder of Game 4, the Rays found innings where they could. Kevin Kelly came in and relieved Jax, then Nick Martinez — the Rays' Game 1 starter and the assumed starter for Game 5 — entered for two innings. Bryan Baker, who hadn't pitched since displaying diminished velocity in the ALCS, made his World Series debut and threw two shutout innings to get the Rays to extras.That nine innings saw the Rays get another break, as a close play at second base resulted in Pratt getting called safe on an attempted steal. The Rays challenged, and the umpires overturned the call after a four-minute replay review, taking away an at-bat with a runner in scoring position for Milwaukee.Safe or out? pic.twitter.com/BMVpb3RmPU— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the Rays' offense was doing little against the Brewers' bullpen. JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe, DL Hall, Trevor Megill and Aaron Ashby combined for 7 1/3 shutout innings.After 2 1/3 innings from Ashby — enough for the left-hander to make MLB history — the Brewers turned to their less foreboding relievers. Antonio Senzatela finished the 11th inning and was followed by Drohan in the 12th. Maybe there's another world in which Ashby stays in and pitches the final four innings, but the Brewers opted to pull him after 31 pitches, eight fewer than he threw to close out the NLCS.Who is Ben Williamson, the Rays' hero?Williamson has been a valuable player for the Rays this year — but not because of his bat. The utility man has provided effective defense at second base and shortstop and has mostly started as a platoon bat against left-handers.The 25-year-old was playing at the College of William & Mary four years ago, and he was drafted by the Seattle Mariners in the second round of the 2023 MLB Draft. Once again, it was his glove that stood out, and that helped him reach the majors in 2025 as Seattle's starting third baseman.Tampa Bay landed Williamson as its return in the three-way Brendan Donovan deal that saw the St. Louis Cardinals All-Star take Williamson's spot with the Mariners. Until Tuesday, it represented another win on the margins for the Rays.With their season on the line, it became something much more.It will be advantage Brewers in Game 5As disappointing as Game 4 was for the Brewers, they have plenty of reason to be confident they can close out the series in five games.First and foremost is presumptive NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski taking the mound, even if he hasn't been quite as dominant across his first three postseason starts as he was in the regular season.Then there's the fact that we don't know who will pitch for Tampa Bay. Martinez was the natural choice for Game 5, and then he threw 33 pitches in Game 4. The default answer now would be a bullpen game, but that's after five of the team's top arms pitched Tuesday.The Milwaukee bullpen, meanwhile, used closer Trevor Megill for only one out, and he needed five pitches. Abner Uribe threw 19 pitches across two innings. Ashby did make an extended appearance, but a primary lesson of this postseason has been "don't underestimate Aaron Ashby."

articles.title: World Series 2026: Controversial ninth-inning replay decision ends Brewers' threat, sets up Rays to win Game 4 in extras
articles.summary: For a moment, the Brewers thought they had the go-ahead run in scoring position in the top of the ninth inning of Game 4 of the World Series.
articles.body:
For a moment Tuesday, the Milwaukee Brewers thought they had the go-ahead run in scoring position in the top of the ninth inning of Game 4 of the World Series.

But an overturned call ended the Brewers' threat, and three innings later, the Tampa Bay Rays secured a walk-off, 4-3 victory in 12 innings to extend the series to Game 5 with Milwaukee holding a 3-1 lead.

With pinch hitter Andrew Vaughn at the plate, Cooper Pratt stole second as the go-ahead run in a 2-2 game with the Brewers trying to secure a 4-0 series sweep. Pratt appeared to slide just under the tag of Richie Palacios, and umpire Tripp Gibson called Pratt safe on a close play.

But Kevin Cash wasn't satisfied with the call. The Rays' manager challenged, setting off nearly four painstaking minutes at Tropicana Field.

As MLB's replay center looked at the play, the Fox broadcast parsed multiple did-he-or-didn't-he angles, debating whether Palacios tagged the tip of his glove on Pratt's left hand as Pratt slid.

One angle looked like he might have. Multiple others did not. Given that the call on the field was safe, the replay had to provide conclusive evidence that Palacios applied the tag in order to determine that Pratt was out.

At the conclusion of the lengthy replay review, home plate umpire James Hoye took the field to deliver a succinct verdict: "After review, the call is overturned. The runner on the field is out."

With that, the Brewers' threat was extinguished, and top of the ninth was over.

Rays walk it off in 12th to force Game 5

The game remained tied 2-2 until the top of the 12th inning, when Pratt hit a solo home run to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead. But the Rays responded with two runs in the bottom of the 12th, and Ben Williamson's walk-off single secured a 4-3 Tampa Bay victory .

The Brewers might or might not have gone on to win Game 4 and the World Series had Pratt been called safe on his ninth-inning steal attempt. But thanks to a savvy challenge by Cash, the Rays didn't have to find out.

Game 5 is scheduled for 8 p.m. ET Wednesday in St. Petersburg, where the Rays will once again look to extend the series and their season.

articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays kept their 2026 World Series hopes alive in Game 4, walking off the Milwaukee Brewers in 13 innings in thrilling fashion.

The Brewers, smelling its first World Series title in franchise history after 22-year-old Cooper Pratt broke an innings-long 2-2 tie with a solo home run in the top of the 13th inning, were just three outs away from celebrating. But after an error allowed Junior Caminero to reach base to start the frame, the Rays finally smelled some life. Liam Hicks made even more believers in Tropicana Field when his single moved Caminero to third base, and Jonny DeLuca told the Brewers, "Not so fast!"
