articles.title: Rays stun Brewers with 2-run rally in 12th inning, force World Series Game 5 with 4-3 win
articles.summary: Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5.
articles.body: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jonny DeLuca and pinch hitter Ben Williamson singled home runs in a stunning 12th-inning rally, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night that forced Game 5. Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th as Milwaukee neared a sweep and its first World Series title. But the Rays, also seeking their first championship, rallied in the bottom half after a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz on Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder against reliever Antonio Senzatela. Liam Hicks singled off Shane Drohan, who relieved in his first appearance since Oct. 15, and DeLuca's single to center drove in pinch runner Cedric Mullins to tie the score at 3. Chandler Simpson's single loaded the bases and Milwaukee employed a five-man infield with the infield in. Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the postseason, hit a chopper over first baseman Jake Bauers and into right field. Game 5 will be Wednesday night at Tropicana Field. Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5. Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one that rebounded to win was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Brewers are left to grapple with only their second loss of the playoffs after 12th-inning unraveling in Game 4
articles.summary: "That loss stings, but it's a part of our story," reliever Aaron Ashby said after Milwaukee's 4-3 loss.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Cooper Pratt could taste it. Wisconsin could, too.

Two ticks after midnight ET, in the nascent moments of Wednesday morning, Milwaukee's teetotaling Gen Z shortstop put a franchise, a city and a state on the brink of a historic rager. Leading off the top of the 12th inning, Pratt lofted a poorly located sweeper five rows beyond the left-field wall to break a 2-2 deadlock. Brewers players poured onto the field in uncontrollable jubilation as the sizable contingent of traveling Sconnies lost their marbles and voices and all semblance of reality.

It was the swing of a lifetime — not to mention the fourth hit of the evening for a 22-year-old rookie.

Three outs from the Tampa Bay Rays. That's all that stood between these Brewers and immortality, between 56 years of heartbreak and catharsis, as this thriller flipped to the bottom of the 12th.

Tampa Bay stormed back to plate a pair in the 12th against reliever Shane Drohan, taking this unhinged Game 4 in walk-off fashion by a 4-3 score . In doing so, the Rays kept their baseball season going for at least one more day .

Math and history remain firmly on Milwaukee's side. No team in World Series history has ever come back from a 3-0 deficit to win it all. For Wednesday's Game 5, the Brewers will hand the rock to Jacob Misiorowski, the NL Cy Young Award favorite. Tampa Bay, on the other hand, has yet to announce a starter. And even if the Rays push this Fall Classic back to American Family Field, winning two straight in that thunderdome is quite a formidable task.

That doesn't lessen the emotional pain of Game 4 for the Brewers. One last gut-punch for the road.

"I think the guys understand it's going to be hard," Brewers skipper Pat Murphy conveyed postgame. "It's going to be hard. You're playing the best team in the American League. They proved it all yearlong, and they came up big today. It's going to be hard."

Similarly difficult, for the Brewers, will be grappling with this loss. Before Tuesday, Milwaukee had not dropped a ballgame in 21 days. The stunned silence in the postgame clubhouse was foreign, unfamiliar. This Brewers team has been such a freight train, such a relentless force of nature , that it felt downright bizarre to watch them trudge off the field in defeat.

"That loss stings, but it's a part of our story," said reliever Aaron Ashby, who set a record in Game 4 by throwing his 18th consecutive scoreless inning , the most by a reliever in MLB postseason history. "I think the boys are fired up to get in here tomorrow."

For most of the evening, though, the prospect of tomorrow felt unlikely.

The two clubs traded punches in the early going. Tampa opened the scoring in the second with a Chandler Simpson RBI double. Pratt answered in the fourth with an RBI double of his own, but Tampa jumped back in front in the bottom half on a missed defensive play from third baseman David Hamilton .

But Hamilton redeemed himself immediately, cranking just his fifth homer of the season to retie things 2-2. And there the contest stayed for about two-and-a-half hours. As the Rays and Brewers swapped zeros, with both bullpen carousels rising to the occasion, Milwaukee's October track record of dramatic comeback after dramatic comeback lingered like a monster under the bed. It was just a matter of time, surely, until an offensive outburst.

Instead, Milwaukee went six straight innings without scoring a run, their longest drought of this postseason.

"We hit seven balls that were above 97 [mph] tonight that got caught," Murphy lamented afterward. "There's a chance that's going to disrupt your flow in your offense."

Even so, the Brewers surged ahead via Pratt, whose massive long ball was momentarily the most consequential play in franchise history. For about 15 minutes, he was the most famous man in Wisconsin.

"Probably one of the coolest swings of my life," he shared after the game, albeit in an understandably subdued tone. "But it's over."

It didn't have to be. Milwaukee's 12th-inning unraveling was self-inflicted.

With nobody out, third baseman Joey Ortiz, one of the most sure-handed defenders in the sport, short-hopped a routine throw to first, which let Junior Caminero reach. In came the rookie Drohan for just his second appearance of these playoffs. He allowed a scorcher to the first batter he faced, catcher Liam Hicks, putting runners on the corners. Jonny DeLuca and Simpson then punched singles up the middle to tie the score and load the bases. Nobody warmed up in the Brewers 'pen; Murphy was saving Misiorowski for Game 5.

Ben Williamson then finished the job, chopping a trampoline ball over a drawn-in infield to give Tampa Bay its first home World Series win since 2008.

Wisconsin, meanwhile, will need to put the champagne and the champagne of beers back on ice for at least one more day.

"We've talked about it a lot as a group, how it's supposed to be hard," Brewers captain Christian Yelich opined. "This stuff is not supposed to be easy. It's supposed to test you."

articles.title: World Series 2026: With pinch-hit, 12th-inning walk-off, Ben Williamson meets the moment in Game 4 and extends the Rays' season at least one more day
articles.summary: “[Manager Kevin] Cash just kind of turned around and said, ‘Get ready to hit,’” Williamson said after his game-winning single.
articles.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It sure wasn't pretty. But the Tampa Bay Rays won't complain.

Ben Williamson delivered the 64th walk-off in World Series history on Tuesday — or, at 12:28 a.m. Wednesday, to be exact — to help the Rays stave off elimination and topple the mighty Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 in a Game 4 that stretched 12 innings over 4 hours, 20 minutes.

For the first 11 innings of this tightly contested ballgame, Williamson sat on the bench and watched as the Brewers tiptoed toward the finish line of the first championship in franchise history. Rookie Cooper Pratt's go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 12th sent the gigantic contingent of Milwaukee supporters at Tropicana Field into ecstasy, within three outs of baseball nirvana.

But when third baseman Joey Ortiz's throwing error enabled Junior Caminero to reach base leading off the bottom of the inning, the window was cracked open for Williamson's specific services to be eventually called upon. And after three singles against lefty Shane Drohan, Williamson represented the final maneuver for manager Kevin Cash to make.

"Cash just kind of turned around and said, 'Get ready to hit,'" Williamson recalled afterward. "Jokingly, in my head, I was thinking, 'Yeah, I've been ready to hit since the fourth or fifth inning."

The 25-year-old, glove-first infielder with zero knocks in this World Series pinch-hit for Victor Mesa Jr. with a simple goal in mind: Put the ball in play. With the bases loaded, nobody out and the game already tied 3-3, Williamson just needed to avoid striking out to have an excellent chance at a favorable outcome.

As such, Cash's swap made sense, considering Mesa is one of the rare Rays with a tendency to whiff, while Williamson embodies the club's greatest strength: making contact. Tampa Bay had the highest contact rate and the lowest strikeout rate in MLB in the regular season. Those skills were on display leading up to Williamson's game-winner, as Liam Hicks, Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson all collected their singles with two strikes.

Hicks punched a 2-2 fastball into left field that moved Caminero to third before Cedric Mullins pinch-ran for him after the third baseman seemed to pull something rounding second (Caminero is expected to be in the lineup for Wednesday's Game 5). DeLuca then smacked a 1-2 cutter into center field to tie the game. With runners on first and second and nobody out, Simpson arrived at the plate in an obvious bunt scenario but missed an attempt and fell into a 2-2 count. Still, the Rays weren't concerned.

"Chan getting down to two strikes, missing the bunts … but we know he's a guy that's going to put the ball in play," Hicks said afterward. "I don't think there's any worry when that happens … like, 'We're out of it. He's going to strike out.' Like, that's not going through anyone's mind. Everyone knows how good he is at putting the bat on the ball."

Sure enough, Simpson smoked a high fastball from Drohan back up the middle for his third hit of the game, which loaded the bases before Cash pressed his final bench button.

But Williamson took a different tact than his teammates. Rather than embarking on a lengthy plate appearance that could bring a punchout into play, he wasted no time. He swung at Drohan's first-pitch fastball.

"You have to be ready to go," shortstop Taylor Walls said afterward. "You never know when your name's going to be called. Those guys stay ready on the bench. That was probably more of a grind for them trying to run up and down the tunnel and taking 30 swings an inning than it was for us playing it. It's tough to stay ready in those spots, and he was ready. He was aggressive. He didn't waste any time there.

"Sometimes the first one's the best one you get, and he got it done."

The winning batted ball from Williamson — blasted into the ground at a minus-20-degree launch angle but with such force that it leapfrogged first baseman Jake Bauers and landed in the right-field grass — was not the genre of glorious game-ender we've seen in recent Fall Classics.

This was not a walk-off homer to end an 18-inning marathon the way Freddie Freeman and Max Muncy have somehow both accomplished, nor was it Freeman's walk-off grand slam to beat the Yankees. This was not Adolis Garcia adding to his epic October heater with a walk-off blast to push Texas toward its first championship. This was not Alex Bregman's single off Kenley Jansen to end an absolute circus of a Game 5 that finished 13-12. Heck, this wasn't even as objectively entertaining as the last time the Rays experienced this specific kind of joy, when Brett Phillips unleashed a special kind of chaos with his walk-off single to win World Series Game 4 in 2020.

This was a far less glamorous ball in play, a high chopper that happened to come in the most ideal of circumstances. But it was all it needed to be. Besides, if the Rays are to become only the second team to rally from down 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, they had to start somewhere.

"There's 26 guys that at some point or another throughout the year have come through in a big spot and helped us win a game, and tonight was no different," said reliever Bryan Baker, whose scoreless eighth and ninth innings helped the Rays hang on long enough to win it in extras.

"Getting to see someone like Benny get a hit to finish off the game and pull out a win for us in the World Series is pretty special to see."

Indeed, the Rays rallied to see another day. Now Tampa Bay must turn the page quickly after the late-night triumph and prepare for another battle Wednesday, looking to extend its season even further.

Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski awaits on the mound in Game 5, while the Rays' own pitching plans, according to Cash, are still unsettled. But whatever combination of hitters and pitchers take the field for the next elimination game, the American League champs aren't going to go down easy.

"We love the challenge," DeLuca said postgame. "We're ready for it, and we love the spot we're in. To get this win tonight and have the momentum on our sides right now — we're going to keep it going into tomorrow."

"We're a team that's capable of winning four," Walls said. "At the end of the day, we think we can win the whole thing. So whether it starts with us down 0-3 and winning four in a row or whether it started with us winning the first one or second one … we have full confidence that we can do it."

articles.title: Christian Yelich’s truth bomb after Game 4 loss explains why he’s Brewers’ captain
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers have faced oodles of adversity during the 2026 MLB playoffs, but this group had not suffered a truly stinging postseason loss until Tue...
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers have faced oodles of adversity during the 2026 MLB playoffs, but this group had not suffered a truly stinging postseason loss until Tuesday night. Just three outs away from winning the first Word Series in franchise history, the Brew Crew imploded in the 12th inning and left Tropicana Field with a 4-3 walk-off loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. Their should-be unconquerable 3-0 Fall Classic advantage now looks a tiny more surmountable following Tampa's thrilling win.

Christian Yelich is not worried about ceding momentum, however. He is using this latest bitter October outcome as motivational fuel for Wednesday's Game 5 clash.

"You're supposed to face adversity," the Brewers' first-ever captain said, per MLB.com's Adam McCalvy. "You have to battle back from it. That's why you celebrate at the end, because that's what it requires out of you. I believe in our room and I believe we're prepared to meet that challenge."

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Yelich speaks on this subject from a place of authority. The 2018 National League MVP and 2019 NL MVP runner-up has endured injuries throughout his 30s and produced the worst campaign of his career in 2026. He has been a boon to the Brewers' momentous playoff run, however, reaching base safely in nine of the 11 postseason games he has played this October.

Pat Murphy and the clubhouse stitched the C on No. 22's uniform in late September, and Christian Yelich has since fulfilled the responsibilities that come with that honor. His leadership was valuable while the Brewers outlasted the San Diego Padres, swept the Los Angeles Dodgers and dazed the Rays, but it will be even more important following Tuesday's loss.

The 34-year-old designated hitter, who went 0-for-3 with two walks in Game 4, must keep his younger teammates focused heading into Game 5. One brutal defeat can turn into a downward spiral. Milwaukee cannot dwell on what it let slip through its fingers.

Joey Ortiz and Jake Bauers must shake off the rough error that led off the bottom of the 12th. Shane Drohan needs to move past the four hits he surrendered. And Pat Murphy cannot allow some of his more scrutinized decisions to rattle him moving forward.

The Brewers have exercised incredible mental strength all playoffs long. They cannot stop now. Yelich will do everything in his power to make sure this team keeps its identity intact for another potential championship-clinching matchup.
